title: A strategic rewrite needs a replaceable seam—not a blank sheet
goal: Scope a high-leverage rewrite around one replaceable bottleneck, then gate rollout on semantic parity, operability, compatibility, and an explicit fallback boundary.
tag: Distinguished Engineer · rewrite strategy · architectural seams
concept:
Imagine renovating a restaurant kitchen while the dining room stays open. Keep the menu, ordering counter, and supplier doors stable; replace the cooking line that causes the queue. A blank-sheet rebuild closes the restaurant and makes every boundary part of the project.

A strategic rewrite begins with a measured bottleneck and a replaceable seam: stable inputs, observable outputs, and an old path that can still accept traffic. The new component earns expansion only when it preserves semantics and gains operational maturity—not when its benchmark looks good. This turns “rewrite the platform” into a sequence of falsifiable decisions: profile, isolate, prove parity, canary, expand, and stop where compatibility or risk says stop.
example: A synthetic query fleet spends 92% of CPU in execution while its SQL front end, planner, and storage contracts are stable. A native execution engine is therefore a plausible seam. On 100 representative queries it uses 41% less CPU, but only 96 results match the legacy engine. The decision is hold the canary: four semantic gaps outweigh the performance win. After fixes reach 100/100 parity, the team routes 5% of eligible traffic, watches correctness, crashes, memory, latency, and fallback rate, then expands only the eligible set. Unsupported connectors remain on the old engine; “90% of eligible traffic” is not misreported as 90% of all traffic.

use_case.when: Use a seam-first rewrite when profiling finds one concentrated bottleneck, the surrounding contracts can stay stable, and the legacy path can remain as a bounded fallback during migration.
use_case.example: Your Spark or Presto estate has accumulated years of planner, connector, security, and user-facing semantics, but most compute cost is concentrated in the local execution layer.
use_case.decision: Replace the execution layer behind its plan and data interfaces. Gate every traffic increase on semantic parity and production controls; keep unsupported workloads explicitly out of scope instead of pulling them into a platform-wide rewrite.

practice: Move through the four evidence states. Predict the decision before reading it, then name the stable seam, the rollout gate, and the stop boundary for one rewrite in your estate.
boundary: This is an original local decision model, not a live Presto or Velox benchmark. Its 100-query corpus, 92% CPU share, 41% saving, parity counts, and traffic percentages are synthetic. A stable interface can still hide semantic coupling; matching outputs does not prove identical performance, security, or failure behavior; and a fallback can become permanent dual-operation debt. Real adoption needs workload-specific tests, shadowing, observability, capacity planning, rollback drills, and human review.

questions: A new engine cuts CPU 41%, but 4 of 100 representative query results differ. What is the correct rollout decision?
Hold traffic and close the semantic gaps
Expand because CPU is the strategic metric
Silent wrong answers are a stop condition. Performance matters only after semantic parity is credible.
Why preserve the SQL surface, planner, and connectors when execution is the measured bottleneck?
Stable boundaries concentrate the change and preserve fallback
A rewrite should avoid all integration tests
A seam narrows blast radius and supports comparison, routing, and rollback; it does not declare adjacent layers perfect.
The new engine carries 90% of eligible traffic. What must an executive update say?
Name the eligibility boundary and the unsupported workloads
Say the migration is 90% complete without qualification
The denominator is part of the evidence. Eligibility exclusions reveal the remaining compatibility and operating cost.

steps.note: Start with a concentrated bottleneck and keep the performance claim separate from correctness.
Name the component boundary and the old path that makes comparison and rollback possible.
Turn parity into a traffic gate; four mismatches mean the canary remains closed.

steps.code: decision={'action':'hold canary','scope':'execution engine only','reason':'4 semantic gaps remain'}
steps.note: Choose the bounded next action rather than widening the rewrite to solve unrelated layers.

walkthrough.limit: This is an original local decision model, not a live Presto or Velox benchmark. Its corpus and metrics are synthetic. Real rollout requires workload-specific semantic, performance, security, resilience, and rollback evidence.

Each state changes one decision variable—bottleneck evidence, parity, canary traffic, then eligibility—so a performance result cannot silently override correctness or scope.
